title: The end of the genetic paradigm of cancer
one_line: A theory/essay piece arguing that the somatic mutation theory (the 'genetic paradigm') of cancer is not supported by accumulated evidence and should give way to tissue-organisational and cell-state explanations.
key_claims: The authors argue that decades of cancer genome sequencing have not delivered the predicted causal account of carcinogenesis, undermining the somatic mutation theory as a general explanation.
They point to widespread 'oncogenic' driver mutations found in histologically normal, non-cancerous tissue as evidence that mutation alone is insufficient for cancer.
They highlight cancers with few or no identifiable driver mutations, and carcinogens that act without mutating DNA, as anomalies the genetic paradigm cannot absorb.

They argue that reversible, non-genetic changes in cell state and tissue organisation (including development-like and gene-regulatory-network attractor dynamics) better account for initiation, progression and occasional reversal of malignancy.
They frame the shift as a Kuhnian paradigm change, arguing that continued patching of the mutation theory with auxiliary hypotheses signals its exhaustion rather than its robustness.
limitations: This is a conceptual/perspective essay, not new experimental data; no primary measurements or statistics are generated.
The proposed alternative framework is argued rather than tested head-to-head against the somatic mutation theory in a predictive experiment.
Evidence cited is selected to illustrate anomalies and is not a systematic review of the cancer genomics literature.
Clinical successes of mutation-targeted therapies are acknowledged as a challenge the argument must accommodate rather than fully resolved.
No operational criteria are given for how a tissue-organisation or cell-state model would be falsified.
open_questions: What prospective experiment would distinguish mutation-driven from cell-state/tissue-organisation-driven carcinogenesis in the same tissue?
Can malignant phenotypes be durably reversed by manipulating cell state alone while driver mutations remain intact?
Why do some mutation-targeted therapies work well if mutations are not the causal driver?
What quantitative framework would predict which normal tissues carrying driver mutations progress to cancer and which do not?
